title: Lovász conjecture
formal: Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path?
definitions: A graph is vertex-transitive if for every u,v there is a bijection of its vertex set preserving adjacency and sending u to v. A Hamiltonian path is an ordering of all vertices without repetition in which consecutive vertices are adjacent; the one-vertex graph is allowed. The target asks for existence, with no requirement to compute the path efficiently. It asks for a path rather than a cycle, and is not restricted to Cayley graphs.

context_blocks.text: Vertex transitivity expresses complete local symmetry, but does not give an obvious global route visiting each vertex once. The Hamiltonian-path conjecture is a classical structural question connecting graph symmetry with spanning paths.

It lies within the atlas’s accepted graph-structure and path scope. Positive results for particular group actions or graph families do not settle the universal statement. The cycle variant has exceptional behavior and is not substituted for the path question.

why: Resolve a canonical connection between graph symmetry and global spanning structure.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

progress.text: The July 2026 revision proves a cycle-length lower bound of \(n^{2/3- o(1)}\) for general connected vertex-transitive graphs; it does not establish Hamiltonian paths.
